Part I

Understand

What a data centre is, what is inside an AI campus, and how heat leaves it.

1

Why build AI data centres in India, what they pay back, and what matters

The questionDoes India need much more AI data-centre capacity? What does the country get in return, what happens if it is not built, and what decides whether a project helps or hurts?

The short answerYes, but on conditions. India hosts ~1.2 W of data-centre capacity per person against ~50 W in the US, must run payments, health and government AI at home, and is exposed to foreign compute and export controls. The payback is large in capital, construction and strategic capability, and small in permanent jobs (~0.2–2.6 per MW). Not building moves the demand abroad rather than removing it; building badly strands GPUs and strains power and water. How and where capacity is built matters more than how much.

1.11.21.31.4
1.1Research · Need

The need: a real gap, softer headline numbers

The popular line is that India makes 20% of the world's data but hosts 3% of its capacity. MeitY has told Parliament that global datasets do not support the 20% figure and that 3% is only indicative. Per person, the gap is clearer and larger.

~1.79 GWlive IT capacity, H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield 1,789 MW, the atlas anchor; Savills and KPMG give up to 1.9); 387 MW added in 2025, +103%
~1.2 Wper person in India, vs ~50 W in the US and ~230 W in Singapore (atlas arithmetic)
100 Mweekly ChatGPT users in India, most served from abroad
2,117global capability centres employing 2.36 M; 1,200+ with AI/ML work; 900+ units in Bengaluru
630 M+UPI transactions a day on domestic infrastructure
38,000+IndiaAI GPUs; users pay ~₹65–67/GPU-hour after the 40% subsidy (lowest bids average ~₹115); ~100,000 targeted

DriverWhy it needs capacity in India

How big by 2030? Forecasts spread three-foldGW of capacity in 2030, by source and source type.

The atlas uses KPMG's 7–7.5 GW as the central case, the Economic Survey's ~4 GW as the downside and Wood Mackenzie's 12 GW as the upside. The power ministry's 26.3 GW of extra AI data-centre load by 2031–32 (17 GW already applied for connection) is a grid-stress scenario in facility power, not a demand forecast. KPMG expects AI to be ~55% of capacity by FY30 and ~65% by FY35.

1.2Research · Dividends

What data centres pay back

Big in capital, construction and strategic capability; small in permanent jobs. The honest employment case rests on what data centres enable, not on who works inside them.

What other hosts learnedFrom courting data centres to conditioning them.

  • Ireland: data centres used 22% of metered electricity in 2024 (5% in 2015), more than all urban homes; Dublin connections paused from 2022; since Dec 2025 new sites must bring matching generation or storage.
  • Singapore: moratorium 2019–22; new capacity only by tender at PUE ≤1.25 and ≥50% green power; a bill to license every site of 3 MW+.
  • Johor: 10 MW (2021) to 5.7 GW planned; data-centre water tariff RM5.33/m³; reclaimed water mandated; water-cooled expansions deferred; ~30% of applications rejected; actual draw ~55% of approved, so operators must use 85% of booked power.
  • Virginia: real construction benefits and local taxes, against the state's largest tax break and household bills that could rise US$14–37 a month by 2040.

Lesson: benefits are front-loaded and diffuse; grid, water and tariff costs are local and long-lived. Social licence depends on data centres paying for, and bringing, their own resources.

CSO Ireland; CRU; IMDA; Johor state reporting; JLARC. reported

1.3Research · Counterfactual

If they are not built, and if they are built badly

The asymmetry favours building, with discipline. Under-building costs strategic capability and value that are hard to recover. Over-building mostly costs investors, unless grid, water or subsidy costs are pushed onto everyone else.

Under-build: the demand goes elsewhere

  • Workloads move, not vanish: to Singapore (rationed), Johor, the Gulf or the US, though India is cheaper to build in (Mumbai ranks among the most cost-efficient markets).
  • Latency and compliance: payments, fraud scoring, health records and government AI cannot easily go offshore; they fall back on small, inefficient enterprise rooms.
  • Forex and value: cloud and AI paid for as imports; ~US$30 bn of domestic construction spend to FY30 lost.
  • Dependency: sovereign model training and government AI rely on foreign capacity that can be repriced, rationed or controlled.
  • GCCs: Bengaluru and Hyderabad lose their pitch against hubs with local GPUs.
  • No global environmental gain: the footprint shifts to other grids, often dirtier or drier (Malaysia ~0.74 kg CO₂/kWh; Johor water-limited).

Over-build or bad build: stranded and strained

  • Idle public compute: the IndiaAI portal had 144 users in Sept 2025 against 34,000+ GPUs (Takshashila); GPUs depreciate in 3–5 years whether used or not.
  • Speculative grid queues: 9.3 GW of the 26.3 GW projection has not even applied; Malaysia's draw was ~55% of approvals.
  • Obsolescence: only 25–30% of existing capacity can be upgraded for AI; halls built for 20–40 kW racks strand as racks pass 100 kW.
  • Bubble dynamics: Sify's CEO warns herd behaviour could create a glut; scholars compare it with the 2000s fibre overbuild.
  • Resource conflict: India's data-centre water is estimated at ~150 bn L (2025) rising to ~358 bn L (2030) (market-research estimate); stressed aquifers turn a national gain into a local cost.

Takshashila Institution (Oct 2025); Communications Today; Reuters; KPMG; arXiv 2606.01575; Mordor Intelligence. reported estimate

1.4Guide · What matters

What matters, in order, and why

Power first, then demand certainty, then water and cooling, then design for density. In Bengaluru, water comes first.

A ranked framework for IndiaEach factor with the reason it ranks where it does.

#FactorWhy it matters
1Firm clean power, and a dateThe binding constraint, ahead of land and capital; AI needs round-the-clock supply and its load swings; 17 GW already queued
2Demand certainty and utilisationGPUs depreciate fast; anchor tenants and pre-leases decide viability; IndiaAI under-use is the warning
3Water and cooling~75% of Indian data centres sit in water-stressed regions; evaporative cooling uses ~12 ML per MW of IT a year at 78% load (10–15 by climate); see chapter 5
4Design for future densityLiquid cooling, >2,000 kg/m² floors, 7 m slab-to-slab, 30–150 kW racks now and headroom for Rubin and Kyber
5Capital and financing~US$1 bn per 150 MW before GPUs; cost of capital and GPU depreciation dominate returns
6Supply chain and GPU accessTransformer shortages; imported cooling and batteries; GPU supply subject to US policy
7Location, fibre and hazards14 cable landing stations at 5 places; coastal flood and cyclone design; inland heat and water resilience
8PolicyState incentives, open access, ISTS waivers, the 2047 tax holiday, DPDP clarity
9Disclosure and social licenceNo state yet requires central water disclosure; Johor and Ireland show opposition follows opacity
10TalentCost-advantaged, but AI data-centre design depth is thin and dominated by foreign firms
11Security and resilienceTier III/IV, ISO 27001/22301: table stakes for banks and government

Bengaluru: water before powerWhere the general framework bends.

  • Today: 31 of Karnataka's 32 private data centres sit in Bengaluru, mostly in the water-stressed east and south-east. WELL Labs estimates ~20 MLD (an upper bound; the atlas's central estimate is 3.4–4.5 MLD, chapter 12). Devanahalli draws groundwater at 169% of recharge.
  • The 1 GW goal on evaporative cooling would need ~34 MLD on site at 78% load; on dry liquid cooling, about 1 MLD (chapter 12).
  • The 2026–31 policy has the right architecture (PUE/WUE reporting, resource mapping, corridors outside the city) but weak price signals: the ₹8 lakh treated-water cap is ~₹3/kL for a 10 MW evaporative site.
  • Recommended: require treated or reclaimed water for new builds above a size threshold; set a WUE ceiling; keep latency-sensitive inference in the city and send GPU-dense training to corridors with surface water and round-the-clock renewables (Vizag, Jamnagar, Chennai); require renewable PPAs to add new supply, as Ireland now does.
  • Bengaluru's natural role: with 900+ GCC units and the deepest AI talent pool, low-latency enterprise inference and fine-tuning.

Newslaundry (Apr 2026); GWD–CGWB 2024; Karnataka policy summaries; atlas chapters 12 and 5. reported

Checklist for judging an AI data-centre projectTick what a project can show. Twelve questions from the research.

Where the sources disagree
  • "20% of data, 3% of capacity" is widely repeated, but MeitY calls the 20% unsupported and the 3% indicative.
  • Capacity baselines (1.5, 1.8, 1.9, 2.2 GW) differ by definition; the government keeps no official count.
  • 2030 forecasts run 4–12 GW (23 GW from an investment house); the 26.3 GW power-side figure is not comparable.
  • Jobs per MW span 0.15–188, from mixing construction, indirect and "ecosystem" jobs with permanent posts.
  • AI GDP claims are about adoption and do not isolate domestic data centres; national water totals come from a market-research firm, not metered data.
  • The Diffusion Rule's rescission was announced, but its formal removal may not have been published; the export regime remains fluid.
  • "Bubble unlikely" views come mainly from property brokers with a commercial interest.

Data centre 101 and the types India builds

The questionWhat is a data centre, and what kinds does India build?

The short answerA data centre is a factory that turns electricity into computing and heat. India's 1,789 MW of IT capacity (Cushman & Wakefield, H1 2026; trackers differ by about ±5%) is mostly colocation in Mumbai, while hyperscale cloud and AI campuses now drive the growth.

2.2Report 1 · Types of data centre, global and Indian

Scale wins, and India is just getting started

A single facility can be "hyperscale", "AI", "Tier III" and "liquid-cooled" at once, because each label answers a different question. Globally, the economics of scale have pushed capacity from company-owned rooms to cloud giants and colocation. India is small and growing very fast.

~103 → 200 GWGlobal data-centre capacity, 2025 → 2030 (JLL, 14% CAGR)
56% → 32%Enterprise on-premises share of capacity, 2018 → 2026 (Synergy)
~50%Mumbai's share of India's live capacity; ~95% of international bandwidth lands there

Type explorerSix business models. Pick one to see how it works, what it costs and who uses it.

Who owns the world's capacityShare of global data-centre capacity (Synergy Research). 2031 is a projection.

Enterprise capacity is flat in absolute terms; its share shrinks because hyperscale grows so fast. Twenty metro markets hold 60% of hyperscale capacity, with Northern Virginia alone at 11%.

Tier III is the commercial standard worldwide and in India. In India an AI or Tier IV build costs up to ₹75 crore/MW, against ₹50–55 crore for Tier III air-cooled (SBI, April 2026).

India by cityMegawatts, H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield). Switch between what runs today and what is coming by 2030.

Type finderAnswer four questions and get the type the series would recommend.

Single point of failure. Fifteen of India's 17 international cables land within about 6 km of Versova beach in Mumbai, carrying about 95% of international bandwidth. New east-coast landings (SEA-ME-WE 6 at Chennai, Google's Vizag gateway) matter more than any incentive.
The money already committed. Google ≈US$15 bn for a 1 GW AI hub at Vizag; Microsoft US$17.5 bn; Amazon US$35 bn+ across India by 2030; Reliance up to 3 GW at Jamnagar; Adani ≈US$100 bn by 2035; TCS HyperVault 1 GW+. These are announcements, not finished capacity.

What India should build, in order

  1. Hyperscale and wholesale colocation campuses in five hubs: Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Noida and Vizag. Pair a coastal cable hub with an inland zone 300–700 km away.
  2. Make every large new build AI-ready: 30–130 kW racks, direct-to-chip liquid cooling, PUE ≤1.35. Avoid speculative GPU halls without anchor tenants.
  3. Sovereign and government AI through PPP, extending the IndiaAI "empanel and subsidise" model rather than state-built facilities.
  4. Renewable-backed campuses with round-the-clock contracts; train AI near renewables, serve inference from metros.
  5. A thin layer of modular edge (0.1–2 MW) in Tier-2/3 cities for 5G, UPI and Indian-language inference.

Not priorities: new large enterprise-owned data centres, Tier IV everywhere, underwater designs.

The short answerRack power jumps from about 8 kW to 120–600 kW. Liquid replaces air at the chip, grid connections move to 132–400 kV, and GPUs become most of the cost.

AI racks are a different machine

A conventional rack draws about as much as a few homes; a GB200 rack draws about as much as a street. That one fact changes cooling, power delivery, grid planning and cost. Per query the footprint is small. The aggregate is not.

India's AI build-out

  • IndiaAI Mission: ₹10,372 crore; 38,231 GPUs onboarded across 14 providers at an average ≈₹65/GPU-hour (March 2026); ~20,000 more announced.
  • Yotta: NM1 Navi Mumbai, Tier IV, 52 MW, 8,192 H100s; B300 and Vera Rubin plans at Greater Noida (announced, not commissioned).
  • Reliance Jamnagar: up to 3 GW plan; 120 MW+ expected online H2 2026; Meta lease ~168 MW.
  • Sify: first Indian DGX-Ready liquid-cooling certification (130 kW/rack), later 200 kW/rack sites.
  • Retrofit reality: a 10× density jump strands floor space, needs new transformers, water loops, >1.3 t floor loading and taller halls. Build liquid-ready shells now.

4

Cooling

The questionHow does heat leave the building, and what does each method cost in power and water?

The short answerCooling towers use the least electricity and the most water (about 1.8 L per kWh of IT; 1.5–2.4 by climate). Dry and liquid systems use almost no water but more power in hot hours.

4Report 3 · Every cooling type, what it costs, what India should build

Removing heat is half the design

Cooling has two halves. Inside the room you pull heat away from the chips with air, rear-door coils, cold plates or immersion. Outside you reject it to the atmosphere with towers, adiabatic coolers or dry coolers. The outside choice decides most of the water bill; the inside choice decides how dense the racks can be.

20–40 kWPer rack: where air cooling stops being practical
$3 bn → $7 bnLiquid-cooling manufacturer revenue, 2025 → 2029 (Dell'Oro)
1 Jan 2028India freezes HFC refrigerant production and use (Kigali)

The cooling chain, chip to atmosphereA modern liquid-cooled AI hall. Teal carries heat in liquid; red is heat leaving; dashed is the residual air path.

Why liquid winsHeat a cubic metre of fluid carries per degree (kJ/m³·K), log scale.

Moving 100 kW with a 10 K rise needs about 8 m³/s of air but only 2.4 L/s of water. That is why fan power and air-handler size collapse once heat is caught at the chip.

Who bought whom (2024–26)

About US$16 bn of deals turned cooling into a strategic choke point. Insist on open interfaces (OCP UQD couplings, CDU controls) to avoid lock-in.

India's HFC phase-down under KigaliSpecify low-GWP refrigerants (R-1234ze, R-513A, R-32) in chillers bought now. Chiller-free W45 designs are the most future-proof.

How the hyperscalers cool

  • Google: liquid-cooled TPUs since 2018; says its Vizag AI hub will use air-cooled (dry) heat rejection.
  • Microsoft: since August 2024 every new design is closed-loop "zero water evaporation", avoiding 125 million L a year per site. Fleet WUE 0.30 L/kWh.
  • Meta: air-assisted liquid cooling (cold plates dumping heat into room air via rear-door coils) in existing halls.
  • AWS: In-Row Heat Exchanger (July 2025) to run GB200 racks in air-cooled halls.

Indian deployments

  • NTT NAV1, Mahape: 4.8 MW immersion + direct-contact cooling (2023), ~30% more efficient.
  • Sify: 130 kW/rack Rabale; 200 kW/rack Chennai and Noida (DGX-Ready).
  • Yotta: RDHx to 50–60 kW, DLC to 80 kW per rack.
  • Local supply: Schneider/Motivair liquid-cooling factory in Bengaluru (2026); Vertiv in Pune (200 W–2 MW+).
  • Leading operators report PUE 1.4–1.5; MeitY AI tenders want <1.35.

Don't build new freshwater-evaporative plants in Chennai, Bengaluru or Gurugram. Don't bet on two-phase immersion until PFAS-free fluids and OEM warranties mature.
